newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks, bonds rise on hopes for steady rates.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks, bonds rise on hopes for steady rates.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks rallied along with the bond market Friday on investors' growing expectations that the Federal Reserve will not raise interest rates next week.
The dollar rallied on new signs of economic weakness in Japan and further worries about Europe's planned single currency.
The Dow Jones industrial average rose 33.47 points to close at 7,687.72. The index had risen as much as 116 points before late-session profit-taking shaved the gains.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines by 1,799 to 938 on active volume of 469.7 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

For the week the Dow finished with a loss of 108.79 points after Monday's 192-point drop, its second worst point loss ever, triggered by remarks from Japan's prime minister on possible selling of U.S. Treasury bonds. The Dow bounced back 154 points on Tuesday.
"Nothing much has happened, but you've travelled a lot of miles in between," said Alfred Kugel, senior investment strategist at Stein Roe & Farnham.
The Dow ended last week at a record high of 7,796.51, a 22 percent rise from its 1997 closing low at 6,391.69 on April 11.
Market analysts attributed the sharp swings to a general nervousness among investors holding big gains after the 10-week rise of over 1,400 points.
"That's what the volatility shows," said James Melcher, president of Balestra Capital. The stock market "is edgy all right, and it ought to be."
On Friday stocks got support from bonds, which broke out of a week-long slide, lifted by the Fed's unexpected purchase in the market of U.S. Treasuries with longer maturities.
The 30-year Treasury rose 15/32, lowering its yield to 6.74 percent from 6.78 percent on Thursday. Prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Wall Street's next hurdle will come Tuesday and Wednesday when Fed policy-makers meet on interest-rate policy. The consensus on Wall Street is that the central bank will leave rates unchanged.
The dollar rose to 114.58 Japanese yen late in New York from 113.15 late on Thursday.

It also hit a 10-day high against the German mark and came within a whisker of its 1997 high, as European officials predicted again that key nations would fail to cut their budget deficits enough to launch the single European currency. The dollar jumped to 1.7385 marks from 1.7255 late on Thursday.
Oil prices rose as traders shrugged off doubts about whether major OPEC producers will be able to restrain exports and focused on more immediate delays in shipments by Iraq.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for August delivery rose 37 cents to $19.46 a barrel.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn prices fell to two-year lows and soybean and wheat prices also fell as near-ideal weather continued in the Midwest and Plains.
Corn for July delivery fell 4 cents to $2.46-1/4 a bushel, the lowest since April 1995. July soybeans closed at $7.87, down 13-1/2 cents a bushel.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 fell 17.6 points to 4,640.3 but was up 46.4 points for the week. Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average closed at 20,523.75, down 101.01 points, but was up 138.21 from last Friday.
